events.text:
🇧🇩🇵🇰🇮🇳 Bangladesh pivots to Pakistan: statement on the Mecca Agreement challenges India
➡️ Bangladesh has announced its intention to consider joining the Mecca Agreement on joint defense, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan on August 7, 2026. This was stated in an interview with the state news agency BSS by the Prime Minister's Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who emphasized that any decision would be made strictly in accordance with national interests and the country's multi-vector foreign policy. The pact stipulates that an armed attack on one signatory is considered an attack on all — in essence, it is the Islamic world's equivalent of NATO's Article 5.
➡️ Over the past year and a half, Dhaka and Islamabad have been rapidly drawing closer. In January, the commander of the Bangladeshi Air Force held talks in Pakistan on the procurement of JF-17 Thunder fighter jets—a Chinese-Pakistani aircraft priced 2–3 times lower than Western equivalents. In May, Pakistan already delivered simulators to Bangladesh for training JF-17 pilots, a step that typically precedes the signing of a contract. Direct flights between Dhaka and Karachi have been resumed, agreements on combating drug trafficking have been signed, and a memorandum on food trade is being prepared. For the first time in decades, Bangladeshi civil servants have gone for training in Pakistan, whereas previously they went exclusively to India.
➡️ For New Delhi, this is a bitter pill. In 1971, thanks to India's military support, East Pakistan gained independence, and Bangladesh was born. This "blood debt" was long regarded as the foundation of Indian dominance in the region. However, after ex-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina fled to India in 2024, relations collapsed. The current leadership is distancing itself from India. Joining the Mecca Agreement would be a strategic breakthrough for Pakistan — an opportunity to enter "India's backyard" through the western flank. Of particular concern to Indian strategists is the proximity of the new military bloc to the Siliguri Corridor—a narrow land bridge connecting mainland India with its northeastern states.

✋ US has lost its dominance in Middle East - American establishment think tank concedes
 
👉 The Middle Eastern order in which the US played the leading role since 1991 is over, stresses Foreign Affairs, the journal of the influential Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) think tank.
It draws parallels between the 1956 Suez crisis that ended the British and French imperial power in the Middle East and Trump's ongoing war against Iran. Though American primacy will not disappear overnight, its fate is sealed, the publication says.
'American hypocrisy and abuse'
🔊 "By nearly every economic, political, and developmental indicator, the Middle East under American domination has performed far worse than any other region," the article reads.
🌏 Israel engaged in numerous wars against its much weaker neighbors and derailed a peace process with Palestine

🌏 Under US stewardship, devastating wars have torn apart Lebanon, Libya, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen
🌏 US-backed neoliberal reforms fueled privatization, enriching elites while leaving much of the population poorer
🌏 Washington’s war on terror encouraged Middle Eastern allies to expand surveillance and crack down on dissent in the name of security
🌏 While small Arab elites prospered, for most people in the region the US-led order brought violence, deprivation, and hopelessness
🌏 The US found itself completely unprepared when Iran pushed back against Trump’s intervention and closed the Strait of Hormuz. US failure to shield its Gulf allies from Iranian attacks has undermined the case for its military presence in the region.
🤥 Donald Trump is unable to stop or reverse the damage. But his successor may bring Iran "into the regional security system as an invested partner" and exert pressure on Israel. All in all, the US will have to work hard to win back the hearts and minds of a region long accustomed to “American hypocrisy and abuse.”
It’s striking to see this admission in a CFR publication, given the think tank’s long-standing reputation for interventionism, American hegemonic ambitions, and serving corporate and elite interests.
Mecca pact signals Uncle Sam is no longer trusted
America’s Middle Eastern partners aren’t waiting around, having lost faith that Uncle Sam will suddenly change. Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia have signed a security pact.

events.text:
❌🚀 US burns through THAAD missiles — replacements stuck until 2027
The US military will not receive new THAAD interceptors until around spring 2027, after its stocks were hammered during the war against Iran, according to analysis based on Pentagon budget documents.
⌛ CSIS noted that previous budget documents projected zero THAAD deliveries to the US between August 2023 and April 2027 — meaning the “arsenal of freedom” apparently needed almost four years to get its next batch of top-tier air-defense missiles.
Pentagon materials also show THAAD responsibility being shifted from the Missile Defense Agency to the US Army in FY2027, while MDA lists no FY2027 funding for the program because the system is being transferred.
The Pentagon’s own budget overview says Operation Epic Fury and Iran’s missile and UAV attacks underscored the need for resilient, layered missile defense.
